newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed, eyeing Kremlin, unveils new Russian party.
newsitem.headline: Lebed, eyeing Kremlin, unveils new Russian party.

text.p: Russia's controversial former security chief and would-be president, Alexander Lebed, said on Friday he was launching a political "third force" that he hopes will one day propel him into the Kremlin.

The gravel-voiced former paratroop general, sacked by President Boris Yeltsin in October for insubordination, said his new party already had substantial financial backing and would aim to forge a broad alliance among diverse social groups.

"We will seek the support of small and medium-sized business, big private industry, the armed forces, the military-industrial complex, the intelligentsia," Lebed told a news conference at the village of Golitsyno, outside Moscow.
He said some banks, companies and wealthy individuals had offered to fund his organisation, which he named the "Russian National-Republican Party" (RNRP).
Lebed, 46, said the RNRP would draw support from both the left and right of Russia's fractured political spectrum but added it would take several months to draw up an official programme.

"We must become an alternative to both the communists and the present democratic apparatchiks," said the charismatic, pug-nosed Lebed, referring to the opposition and Yeltsin's Kremlin administration.
His new party is closely linked to the "Honour and Motherland Movement", whose conference in Golitsyno on Friday provided the stage for Lebed's announcement.

Lebed, shunned by Russia's rulers since being fired as secretary of the policy-making Security Council, needs to build a strong political base if he is ever to realise his ambition of succeeding Yeltsin in the Kremlin.

In an interview published on Friday in the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily Lebed said Yeltsin was still a sick man and should resign. The 65-year-old president returned to the Kremlin on Monday after a heart bypass operation on November 5.
Yeltsin says he now feels well and is again in full control of the vast country but Lebed told reporters the next few months would show whether the president was really up to the task.
Lebed came a solid third in a first round of voting in the presidential election last June and later backed Yeltsin in the run-off on July 3 to defeat a strong communist challenge.

Yeltsin showed his gratitude by drafting Lebed onto his team. In power, Lebed helped seal a peace accord with rebel leaders in breakaway Chechnya, ending 21 months of bloody fighting there, but his strong ambition earned him many enemies.
Yeltsin dramatically sacked Lebed after Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused the security chief of planning a coup.

On Friday, Lebed accused Yeltsin and his government of lacking a long-term strategy for tackling Russia's economic and social problems. The result, he said, was high taxes, constantly changing laws and a lack of "fair play" in business.
He also called for an overhaul of the constitution, saying the president should share some of his powers with parliament.
"We view as appropriate a constitutional reform which would transform the existing super-presidential republic into a normal republic run by president and parliament," he said.
Lebed said that presidential powers should be limited to naming a prime minister, directing foreign policy and controlling the defence, interior and security forces.
